rubric_v1_gloss: “No fault greater than the wish to be getting.”
source_scope: Laozi 46's third fault, against contentment; ch. 44 links large stores with loss.

teaching.quote: … no fault greater than the wish to be getting. Therefore the sufficiency of contentment is an enduring and unchanging sufficiency.
Who loves large stores Gives up the richer state. … Who knows to stop Incurs no blame.

limits: This does not condemn earning or acquiring as such, and the text sets no threshold for 'sufficient'.

id: taoist|laozi_46_faults|To be discontented with one's lot
virtue: To be discontented with one's lot
rubric_v1_gloss: “No calamity greater than to be discontented with one's lot.”
source_scope: Laozi 46's second fault, against the 'sufficiency of contentment'; ch. 44 adds knowing when to stop.

teaching.quote: 2. There is no guilt greater than to sanction ambition; no calamity greater than to be discontented with one's lot; … Therefore the sufficiency of contentment is an enduring and unchanging sufficiency.
Who is content Needs fear no shame. Who knows to stop Incurs no blame.

limits: The text does not define what one's lot is, and the case of real deprivation is unresolved.

rubric_v1_gloss: “There is no guilt greater than to sanction ambition.”
source_scope: Laozi 46's first craving fault in Legge's rendering, set beside the war-horse image and contentment.

teaching.quote: 46. 1. When the Tao prevails in the world, they send back their swift horses to (draw) the dung-carts. When the Tao is disregarded in the world, the war-horses breed in the border lands. 2. There is no guilt greater than to sanction ambition; … Therefore the sufficiency of contentment is an enduring and unchanging sufficiency.
Who cleaves to fame Rejects what is more great; …

limits: This reading depends on Legge's rendering. It does not condemn every goal or the act of earning a living.
